subject: SCIENCE
name: Light
summary: Reflection, mirrors, and the eye that has to make sense of it all.
source: NCERT Class 8 Science, syllabus topic coverage only

questions.stem: What does the law of reflection state about the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection?
choices: They are equal, and both are measured from the normal
The angle of reflection is always twice the angle of incidence
The angle of reflection is always zero
questions.solution: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and both are measured from the normal — the line drawn perpendicular to the surface at the point where the ray strikes. Measuring from the surface instead of the normal is the single most common error in this chapter, and it turns every answer into its complement.

questions.stem: Which part of the eye controls the amount of light entering it?
questions.solution: The iris is the coloured ring of muscle that widens or narrows the pupil, so it controls how much light gets in — which is why your pupils shrink in bright sunlight. The cornea bends the light on the way in, the retina is the screen the image lands on, and the optic nerve carries the signal to the brain.

questions.stem: Which set of properties correctly describes the image formed by a plane mirror?
choices: Virtual, erect, the same size as the object, and laterally inverted
Real, inverted, and smaller than the object
Real, erect, and larger than the object
Virtual, inverted, and smaller than the object
questions.solution: A plane mirror gives a virtual image — it cannot be caught on a screen, because the light only appears to come from behind the mirror. It is upright, exactly the same size as the object, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, and laterally inverted, which is why the writing on an ambulance is printed back to front.

questions.stem: Why can you not see your reflection in a painted wall, even though light reflects from it?
choices: Its surface is rough, so parallel rays scatter in many directions — diffuse reflection
Walls absorb all the light that falls on them
The law of reflection does not apply to walls
Light travels too fast to reflect from a wall
questions.solution: The law of reflection holds at every single point on the wall. The difference is that a rough surface presents normals pointing in many directions, so parallel incoming rays leave in scattered directions and no image forms. A mirror is smooth enough that all the normals are parallel, so the reflected rays keep their arrangement. This is regular versus diffuse reflection, and it is a fact about the surface, not about the law.

questions.stem: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror at an angle of 30° to the mirror surface. What is the angle of reflection?
questions.solution: Angles in this chapter are measured from the NORMAL, not from the surface. If the ray makes 30° with the surface, it makes 90° − 30° = 60° with the normal. So the angle of incidence is 60°, and by the law of reflection the angle of reflection is also 60°. The answer 30° is what you get by taking the given angle at face value, which is exactly what the question is testing.

questions.stem: Two plane mirrors are placed at right angles to each other. How many images of an object placed between them are formed?
questions.solution: For two mirrors meeting at an angle θ, the number of images is (360/θ) − 1 when that division comes out whole. Here θ = 90°, so 360/90 = 4 and the number of images is 3. Each mirror forms one image directly, and the third is formed by light bouncing off both.

questions.stem: Two plane mirrors are inclined at 60° to each other. How many images are formed?
questions.solution: Using the same rule, 360/60 = 6, so the number of images is 6 − 1 = 5. As the angle between the mirrors shrinks, the count grows — which is why two mirrors placed nearly parallel, as in a barber's shop, give a corridor of images that seems to go on forever. At exactly 0° the formula would divide by zero, which is the mathematics agreeing that the images become infinite.

questions.stem: A ray of light falls on a plane mirror. If the mirror is rotated by 10° while the incident ray is kept fixed, by how much does the reflected ray turn?
questions.solution: Rotating the mirror by 10° rotates the normal by 10° as well, which changes the angle of incidence by 10°. Since the reflected ray sits at the same angle on the other side of the normal, it swings by 10° from the normal moving plus another 10° from the angle changing — 20° in total. This doubling is the principle behind the mirror galvanometer, where a small rotation is read as a large movement of a light spot.

questions.stem: A girl stands 2 m in front of a plane mirror. What is the distance between her and her image?
questions.solution: The image in a plane mirror forms as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, so her image is 2 m behind the glass. The distance from her to it is therefore 2 + 2 = 4 m. Answering 2 m confuses her distance from the MIRROR with her distance from the IMAGE, which is the point of the question.

questions.stem: A boy walks towards a plane mirror at 1 m/s. At what speed does his image approach him?
questions.solution: As he moves 1 m closer to the mirror, his image moves 1 m closer to the mirror from the other side, so the gap between them closes by 2 m for every 1 m he walks. Relative to him, the image approaches at 2 m/s. Relative to the MIRROR, though, the image is still only moving at 1 m/s — the question asks for the speed relative to him, and which reference point you are using decides the answer.

questions.stem: What is the shortest plane mirror in which a person 170 cm tall can see their whole reflection?
questions.solution: A mirror only needs to be half the person's height. Light from the top of the head reaches the eye after striking the mirror exactly halfway between the eye and the top of the head, and light from the feet strikes it halfway between the eye and the feet. Those two points are 170/2 = 85 cm apart, so 85 cm of mirror is enough. Remarkably, the answer does not depend on how far away the person stands — moving back changes where the mirror must be placed, but not how long it must be.

questions.stem: Why is a convex mirror, rather than a plane mirror, used as the rear-view mirror in vehicles?
choices: It always gives an erect, diminished image and covers a much wider field of view
It magnifies distant vehicles so they are easier to see
It shows the true distance of vehicles more accurately than a plane mirror
It forms a real image that can be projected onto the windscreen
questions.solution: A convex mirror bulges outward, so reflected rays spread apart and gather a much wider scene into the same piece of glass — which is what a driver needs. The image is always erect and smaller than the object, and always virtual. The cost is exactly the point of the warning printed on such mirrors: because objects appear smaller, they seem further away than they are, so the mirror trades accurate distance for coverage.
